catalog_quote: Il n'existe pas d'étude exhaustive de l'accent touareg. On peut cependant donner quelques indications pour guider ceux qui désirent obtenir une bonne prononciation de la langue touarègue. 1) L'accent touareg est un accent dynamique faible et accompagné d'un ton haut, 2) La place de l'accent varie selon la structure de la phrase (l'accent n'a donc pas de rôle distinctif; il n'existe pas de paires minimales de mots distingués par la place de l'accent, sauf par accident absolu), 3) Les groupes enclitiques jouent un grand rôle, 4) Les temps intensifs ont un accent particulier ... Accent sur la pénultième. La majorité des noms singuliers, p.ex. akắtab, abắyoy, eyắtem ... Accent sur l'antépénultième. Les pluriels à désinence. Les pl.1 gardent donc l'accent sur la même syllabe que le singulier. ... Les temps simples des verbes. On peut dire que les deux temps simples des verbes ont un accent antépénultième latent, car même les formes dissyllabes déplacent l'accent sur une un satellite précédent ou une conjonction précédente dès que cela est possible. ... Accent sur l'ultième. Les mots qui portent l'accent sur l'ultième sont d'espèces exceptionnelles ... Accent fixe dans les temps intensifs. Le parfait intensif et l'imparfait intensif positif reçoivent l'accent sur une syllabe fixe, quelle que soit la structure syllabique de la forme ou de la phrase.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: taya1257 Tayart Tamajeq is not in the catalog. The single searched title, Aikhenvald & Nientao 1988 'On accent in Tamasheq' (Russian, 3-page postgraduate-conference abstract, pp. 3-5, Glottolog 116223), is real (confirmed from Aikhenvald's own CV) but has no digital copy anywhere I could reach: print only, medium priority. In compensation this search of works with stress in the title located and read a first-hand statement for exactly the Niger dialects (tayert/Kel-Fərwan and tawellemmet): Prasse, Alojaly & Mohamed 2003, Dictionnaire touareg-français (Niger), Tome I, 'Note sur l'accent touareg' pp. XX-XXII (archive.org copy saved, pages rendered and read from the image): non-distinctive high-tone weak accent on the enclitic group; penultimate on most singular nouns and internal plurals, antepenultimate on suffixed plurals, vowel-final nouns and simple verb tenses (with leftward shift onto proclitics), final only on a closed exceptional list, fixed morphological accent in intensive tenses. Also saved Prasse 1972 Tahaggart grammar accent section (other variety, pitch accent with three grades, non-phonological). Not obtained: Kossmann 2011 A Grammar of Ayer Tuareg (high priority, the modern grammar of this exact variety), Louali & Philippson 2005 Faits de Langues 26 doi:10.1163/19589514-02601003 (Brill bot wall, medium). discovery relied on Glottolog, Crossref, archive.org APIs.

new_statements.translation: 1) The Tuareg accent is a weak dynamic accent accompanied by a high tone, 2) The place of the accent varies according to the structure of the phrase (the accent therefore has no distinctive role; there are no minimal pairs of words distinguished by the place of the accent, except by pure accident), 3) Enclitic groups play a large role [...] Accent on the penultimate. The majority of singular nouns, e.g. akắtab, abắyoy, eyắtem [...] Accent on the antepenultimate. Plurals with a suffix. Suffixed plurals thus keep the accent on the same syllable as the singular. [...] The simple tenses of verbs. One can say that the two simple verb tenses have a latent antepenultimate accent

Every segment of the reported quote is on the page verbatim at the stated locator: p. XX, heading 'Note sur l'accent touareg', opening paragraph '1) L'accent touareg est un accent dynamique faible et accompagné d'un ton haut, 2) La place de l'accent varie selon la structure de la phrase (l'accent n'a donc pas de rôle distinctif; il n'existe pas de paires minimales de mots distingués par la place de l'accent, sauf par accident absolu), 3) Les groupes enclitiques jouen…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent (a weak dynamic accent realised as high pitch) is non-contrastive and its position is fixed by morphological category and by the enclitic group, not by syllable weight: most singular nouns (and internal plurals, feminines in -t, noun+possessive groups) are accented on the penult; suffixed plurals keep the accent on the same stem syllable as the singular (so surface antepenult), vowel-final singulars, verbal nouns and the two simple verb tenses take antepenultimate accent (the verb's 'latent' antepenult accent moves onto a preceding satellite or conjunction when possible); a closed set (kălá 'no', wălá 'nothing', numerals 2-10, deictic suffixes, disyllabic interjections, French loans, W plurals that lost -a) has final accent; the intensive perfect and positive intensive imperfect have a fixed stem accent regardless of phrase structure (last stem syllable in conj. I-II-IV, e.g. yəlmâd 'he has learned'; first stem syllable in the intensive imperfect, e.g. yəlámmăd).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned: suffixed-plural + possessive groups such as iyătemăn-in carry 'un accent secondaire antérieur' (p. XX); and 'Quand la syllabe accentuée est antérieure à l'antépénultième, cette dernière reçoit pourtant un accent secondaire' (p. XXII, e.g. itîkəlăntif, tâbăragăn).
new_statements.exceptions: Final accent in an exceptional closed set (p. XXII): kălá 'non', wălá 'rien', kəllú 'tout' (Arabic), numerals 2-10 (əssín, kărắḍ.. mărắw), deictic suffixes -en/-naḍ/-nin/-di, măndám, many disyllabic interjections (kăbắt!), French loans (fărtí, kăntí, mušé, otél), and in tawallammat plurals that lost the ending -a (təfert/šifír). Intensive tenses keep a fixed accent whatever the phrase structure. Weak verbs ending in a vowel accent 'comme s'ils n'avaient pas perdu une syllabe'. The authors open by saying no exhaustive study of Tuareg accent exists.
new_statements.domain_note: The accentual unit is the word or the enclitic group (noun + possessive pronoun, verb + object clitics, preposition + pronoun): with a possessive the accent moves toward the end of the group while remaining penultimate (akătáb-in, akătab-nắsăn); the verb's antepenult accent shifts leftward onto a preceding satellite/conjunction (ád-yəlməd, wər-(y)əlmed, ás yəlmăd). Statement is for the Niger Tuareg of the dictionary (Y = tayart of the Kel-Fərwan, W = eastern tawallammat), with W/Y-specific forms flagged; the authors call it a guide to pronunciation rather than an exhaustive account.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Prasse, Alojaly & Mohamed 2003) is a dictionary of Niger Tuareg based, per its Préface p. V, on two dialects: Y = tayərt of the Kel-Fərwan (Aïr) = Tayart Tamajeq taya1257 [thz] (informant Ghabdouane Mohamed), and W = eastern tawəlləmmət of the Kəl-Əylal = Tawallammat Tamajaq [ttq] (informant Ghoubeïd Alojaly). The 'Note sur l'accent touareg' is written for Tuareg generally with Y/W-specific forms flagged by superscript sigla; a few of its example rows are marked W only. The Tayart-specific grammar (Kossmann 2011, 'Ayer Tuareg') could not be opened. Prasse 1972 held by the project describes Tahaggart (thv), not this language.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Prasse et al. 2003 statement (non-contrastive weak dynamic accent with high tone, position varying with phrase structure, enclitic groups, penultimate default on most singular nouns and internal plurals, shift within the possessive enclitic group). It is derivative: the accent passage is a quotation of Prasse 1972 (Tahaggart Manuel) and Prasse et al. 2003 (the Niger dictionary already in the catalog record), so it adds no independent Tayart data; it adds only the Chaker 1989 framing (no phonologically relevant intensity accent in Berber) and the three-grade (principal/secondary/tertiary) description from Prasse 1972. It omits the antepenultimate, final and intensive…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand summary (quoting Prasse 1972 and Prasse, Alojaly & Mohamed 2003): Tuareg accent is a weak dynamic accent with a high tone, non-distinctive (no minimal pairs), its position varying with phrase structure and computed over the enclitic group; penultimate on most singular nouns, feminine -t nouns, Arabic loans in -ǎt and internal plurals; with a possessive pronoun the accent moves to the end of the enclitic group and stays penultimate (ifukan-nắsǎn, akắtáb-in, eɣatém-net); suffixed plurals + possessive also penultimate with an inner secondary accent; monosyllabic preposition + possessive (dát-əs) and most polysyllabic pronouns (nắkku, nǎkkắnǎy) listed as further cases. The thesis also cites Chaker (1989) that Berber syllables differ in intensity but this 'does not imply the existence of an intensity accent with phonological value', and adds its own view that Tuareg accent is only of diachronic/comparative interest (p. 42). The thesis does not reproduce Prasse et al.'s antepenultimate, final and intensive-tense cases.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Quotes Prasse 1972: three grades, 'accent principal' (high tone + slight dynamic increase), 'accent secondaire' (mid tone), 'accent tertiaire' (low tone); the distinction between secondary and tertiary is 'un problème de rythme'. Example Iɣằtemắn-in / iɣằtemǎn-nắsǎn 'avec un accent secondaire intérieur' (p. 42).
new_statements.exceptions: Point 4 (from Prasse 1972): intensive tenses have a particular accent whose exact nature 'attend toujours sa définition', apparently a high tone plus a light treatment of long vowels. No final-accent list or antepenultimate cases are reproduced in the thesis.
new_statements.identity_note: Modi 2022 covers the two principal Niger parlers, tawəlləmmət (sigle W) and tayərt (sigle Y, the parler of the Kel-Ayər/Aïr), the same dialect basis as the Prasse, Alojaly & Mohamed 2003 dictionary from which its corpus and its accent passage are taken (p. 10). The accent points 1-4 are quoted from Prasse 1972, whose primary data are Tahaggart (Algeria); Modi applies them to Tuareg generally.

tone_statements.citation: Kossmann, Maarten. 2007. The borrowing of aspect as lexical tone classes: y-initial Tuareg verbs in Tasawaq. Studies in African Linguistics 36(2): 151-165. doi:10.32473/sal.v36i2.107302
tone_statements.quote: Different from the other Northern Songhay languages and Tuareg, Tasawaq is a tone language. ... In addition to the difference in vowel length and quality, there is also an accentual difference between Short Perfective and Long Perfective in Tuareg (for a description of the intricate accent system of Tuareg, see Heath 2006). In Tasawaq borrowings from Tuareg, the accent is regularly reinterpreted as a High tone, while Tuareg unaccentuated syllables receive a Low tone. ... there are no lexical accentual verb classes in Tuareg.
tone_statements.locator: p. 152 sec. 1 first sentence; p. 157 sec. 3
tone_statements.summary: Tuareg (Ayer forms) treated as non-tonal, with an accent system: ShP accent on first syllable, LoP fixed accent on the lengthened last vowel; Tuareg accent > Tasawaq H tone. ~18 accent-marked forms.

sources.quote: The Long Perfective aspect in Tuareg is morphologically derived from the Short Perfective. The distinction lies in the lengthening of a short central vowel (schwa or a) to a long peripheral vowel (i/u or a) and the insertion of a fixed accent on the lengthened vowel. In the 3SG:M forms of the types of verbs which lie behind the Tasawaq y-initial verbs this means that in Short Perfective forms the accent is on the first syllable, while in Long Perfective forms it is on the last syllable. [...] there are no lexical accentual verb classes in Tuareg.
sources.note: Secondary: the Tuareg accent facts are cited from Heath 2006 ('for a description of the intricate accent system of Tuareg, see Heath 2006', p.157), Prasse 1972-4 and Prasse et al. 2003; not the author's own description. Consistent with the catalog's taya1257 'morphological' accent kind (accent placement fixed by the aspectual form, no lexical accent classes). Also states 'in many Tuareg correspondents of these verb types the accentuation in Long Perfectives and in Short Perfectives are the same, at least in 3SG:M forms' (p.161).

sources.citation: Kossmann, Maarten. 2007. The borrowing of aspect as lexical tone classes: y-initial Tuareg verbs in Tasawaq. Studies in African Linguistics 36(2): 151-165. doi:10.32473/sal.v36i2.107302
sources.quote: Different from the other Northern Songhay languages and Tuareg, Tasawaq is a tone language. ... In addition to the difference in vowel length and quality, there is also an accentual difference between Short Perfective and Long Perfective in Tuareg (for a description of the intricate accent system of Tuareg, see Heath 2006). In Tasawaq borrowings from Tuareg, the accent is regularly reinterpreted as a High tone, while Tuareg unaccentuated syllables receive a Low tone. ... there are no lexical accentual verb classes in Tuareg.
sources.locator: p. 152 sec. 1 first sentence; p. 157 sec. 3
sources.note: Tuareg (Ayer forms) treated as non-tonal, with an accent system: ShP accent on first syllable, LoP fixed accent on the lengthened last vowel; Tuareg accent > Tasawaq H tone. ~18 accent-marked forms.
